blocks.label: The brief
heading: Turn a broad vision
into an everyday product.
blocks.intro: A private founder and two team members approached me with a broad idea: let people choose where to work each day, across a network of workspaces. I helped define, research, design and test the mobile experience, working with the founders and developers through to production.

items.label: Employee need
items.title: Flexibility without isolation.
items.text: Employees wanted less commuting and more choice, without losing the connection of working around other people.

items.label: Business goal
items.title: Adoption that supports efficiency.
items.text: Companies were the paying customers. The business aimed to reduce underused office space while preserving engagement. My focus was an employee experience worth using.

blocks.text: My scope: product definition, user and market research, competitive analysis, core flows, UI, prototyping, user testing and stakeholder presentations.

blocks.label: Research / Understanding the workday
heading: Less commuting.
More connection.
blocks.intro: I combined interviews and short surveys with stakeholder conversations and competitive research to connect daily employee friction with business needs.

items.text: felt disconnected from their team when working from home
would be happy to meet new people while working

blocks.text: Reported in the original project research. Sample size and recruitment details are not available in the case-study record; these are directional signals, not population estimates.
“I love working from home, but sometimes I miss the energy of being around my team.”

figure.alt: Original competitor comparison board: Envoy, Robin and OfficeSpace compared by unique value proposition, company advantages and company disadvantages, on sticky notes
figure.caption: Original competitor comparison

text.text: I benchmarked hybrid-workspace products to compare shared capabilities and identify an opportunity to connect booking with belonging.
The original direction focused on reserving a desk. User conversations led me to expand it: knowing who planned to be there could also influence the choice of workspace.

blocks.label: How might we
heading: Help employees choose where to work with flexibility and belonging, while helping companies use office space more efficiently?

blocks.label: Alignment & project kickoff
heading: Make the direction testable
before making it bigger.
blocks.intro: The founder challenged the added development effort and feasibility of the social layer. I presented the user needs and potential product value. We agreed to prototype and test the direction before moving into development.

figure.alt: Original flow exploration: a booking flow chart starting from the Where button, shown in a recorded project working session with the team on a video call
figure.caption: Original flow exploration and project working session

text.text: The social layer added product complexity and development effort. I had to balance individual productivity with connection on a small mobile screen.
I shaped the core flows, checked feasibility with developers and validated priorities with stakeholders.

blocks.label: Key solution / Booking
heading: One clear place to start.
Three steps toward a desk.
blocks.intro: I designed the core flow for the morning, before leaving for work: a prominent Where action, workspace discovery and a space-detail view.

phone.alt: Second Office home screen: a large blue Where button at the centre of a faded map, with an invitation from a colleague below

items.title: Start with Where
items.label: A clear entry point
items.text: The morning task needed an obvious starting action. Inspired by Shazam, I gave Where visual priority. This was a design intention, not a measured speed improvement.

phone.alt: Second Office map screen: workspaces across lower Manhattan, with a Mooza Space card showing who plans to be there

items.title: Explore places & people
items.label: People in the choice
items.text: The research connected flexibility with belonging. Showing people on the map brought that context into workspace discovery, before choosing a place.

phone.alt: Second Office workspace detail screen: photo of Moooza Space, amenities, a desk price of $40 a day and a Take a seat button

items.title: Review a workspace
items.label: Context before booking
items.text: The detail view combines amenities, people and price. The booking action sits beside the price, keeping cost visible at the point of commitment.

phones.alt: Get Together screen with the Mooza workspace circle empty and a row of contacts above it
phones.caption: Choose a workspace

phones.alt: Get Together screen with four contacts dragged into the Mooza workspace circle, ready to be invited
phones.caption: Invite others to join

text.text: The workspace is the shared destination: people drag contacts into its circle, then continue to invite them. This makes the proposed group visible around a place. Connections can extend beyond an immediate team.
My hypothesis: visible work plans could reduce the need for several conversations and delayed replies in the morning. Visibility helps with the choice; an invitation makes it actionable.

blocks.label: The wider product
heading: Designed end to end.
blocks.intro: Onboarding, connections, reservations and profiles were part of the same experience. The screens shown here all reached production.

items.label: Prototype validation
items.text: Employees from different companies tested the prototype. Feedback highlighted the simplicity of booking and the appeal of GetTogether. Testing covered the app as a whole and supported moving into development.

items.label: Production outcome
items.text: The app, including the social features shown here, reached production and was used outside testing. It was live for a limited period before the company closed. I do not have verified adoption or retention figures to report.

blocks.label: What I learned
heading: Designing the transaction was only part
of designing the workday.
blocks.text: The project taught me to consider both the individual task and its social context, and to make a new direction tangible and testable when its added scope raises questions.

blocks.label: AI in the process
blocks.text: I also used AI to support exploration across research, competitive analysis and early concepts.
